Platform-adapted wide character code unit used by GoldenDict. On Windows (__WIN32), gd::wchar is an unsigned int intended to hold UCS-4 code points; on non-Windows it aliases the native wchar_t. Developers should treat it as a Unicode scalar value container. Size and ABI differ across platforms.

Platform-adapted wide string type. On Windows, gd::wstring is std::basic_string<gd::wchar> (effectively UTF-32/Unicode code points stored as unsigned int). On non-Windows, it aliases std::wstring. Use it for Unicode-aware processing that should be UCS-based on Windows and native wchar_t-based elsewhere.

functions.name: Utf8::encode
functions.signature: size_t Utf8::encode( wchar const * in, size_t inSize, char * out );
functions.description: Encodes a sequence of UCS-4 code units (wchar) into UTF-8 bytes. Writes into the provided out buffer and returns the number of bytes written. The output is not null-terminated. Use when you have raw wide-character data and need its UTF-8 representation without allocations.
requirements: in must point to at least inSize wide characters.
out must point to a buffer of at least inSize * 4 bytes.
The function does not append a terminating '\0'; callers must add it if needed.
in and out must be non-null when inSize > 0.
Callers should not assume any internal state; the function is pure with respect to its inputs.

functions.name: Utf8::encode
functions.description: Convenience overload that encodes a wstring (UCS-4/32) into a UTF-8 std::string. Intended for non time-critical code; performs allocation and returns the encoded bytes as a string. Guaranteed not to throw (per throw()).
requirements: Input wstring must be a valid sequence of wide characters.
No exceptions are thrown; callers should not rely on exceptions for error reporting.
Returned string is not guaranteed to be null-terminated beyond standard std::string invariants.

functions.name: Utf8::decode
functions.signature: long Utf8::decode( char const * in, size_t inSize, wchar * out );
functions.description: Decodes a buffer of UTF-8 bytes into UCS-32 wide characters. Writes decoded characters into out and returns the number of wide characters written. Returns -1 if the input UTF-8 sequence is invalid. Output is not null-terminated. Use when you need a low-level, allocation-free decode.
requirements: in must point to at least inSize bytes of UTF-8 data.
out must point to a buffer that can hold at least inSize wide characters.
The function returns -1 on invalid UTF-8; callers must check for -1 before using the output.
The function does not append a terminating L'\0'; callers must add it if needed.
in and out must be non-null when inSize > 0.

functions.name: Utf8::decode
functions.signature: wstring Utf8::decode( string const & ) THROW_SPEC( exCantDecode );
functions.description: Convenience overload that decodes a UTF-8 std::string into a wstring (UCS-32). Intended for non time-critical code; performs allocation and returns the decoded wide string. Throws exCantDecode if the input is not valid UTF-8.
requirements: Input string must contain UTF-8 encoded data; otherwise exCantDecode is thrown.
Callers that cannot allow exceptions must be prepared to catch exCantDecode.
Returned wstring follows standard wstring invariants; it is not null-terminated beyond those invariants.

functions.name: Utf8::isspace
functions.description: Locale-independent whitespace test suitable for processing UTF-8 byte streams without locale interference. Intended to behave consistently across platforms, unlike std::isspace. Typically used on individual input bytes or code units when tokenizing or skipping ASCII whitespace around UTF-8 text.
requirements: c should be the integer value of a single character/code unit (typically a byte) to test for whitespace.
Behavior is independent of the current C locale; callers should not rely on locale effects.
Only tests the single code unit provided; it does not interpret multi-byte UTF-8 sequences.

functions.name: gd::__nativeToWs
functions.description: Converts a native Windows wide-character string (wchar_t*, UTF-16) to gd::wstring (on Windows, std::basic_string<unsigned int> representing Unicode code points). Intended primarily to support the GD_NATIVE_TO_WS macro, which adapts L"..." literals to a const gd::wchar* for APIs expecting gd::wstring data. Use this to transform UTF-16 sequences (possibly including surrogate pairs) into a UCS-like code-point representation before Unicode-aware processing. Details of error handling for invalid UTF-16 input are not documented.
requirements: Available only on Windows builds where __WIN32 is defined (the function is conditionally declared).
str must point to a valid, null-terminated wchar_t string.
Input is expected to be UTF-16-encoded wide characters as produced by L"..." literals on Windows (inferred from comments and usage).

When used via GD_NATIVE_TO_WS(str), the returned pointer comes from a temporary gd::wstring’s c_str(); it remains valid only until the end of the full expression. Do not store or retain that pointer beyond the immediate call (inferred from macro semantics).
Behavior for invalid or ill-formed UTF-16 sequences is not specified; error reporting is unknown.

functions.name: exName::what
functions.signature: virtual const char * what() const throw()
functions.description: Returns a C-string description of the exception. This function is generated by the DEF_EX and DEF_EX_STR macros for whatever exception class name is supplied as exName. In DEF_EX, it returns the literal exDescription. In DEF_EX_STR, it returns the internal string buffer built as "exDescription + ' ' + value_". Intended for use via std::exception::what().
requirements: Function is noexcept as indicated by throw() and must not throw.
Returned pointer is valid for the lifetime of the exception object; do not use it after the object is destroyed.
In the DEF_EX_STR variant, the returned pointer refers to the internal std::string buffer; do not store it beyond the object’s lifetime or attempt to modify it.

data_types.description: A byte sequence encoded using UTF-8. May contain any Unicode scalar values encoded per RFC 3629. Inputs may also be arbitrary bytes that are not valid UTF-8; decoders should handle and report invalid sequences appropriately. Examples include plain ASCII text (valid UTF-8 subset) and multibyte sequences for non-ASCII code points.
